cleanIntro: Henry's own H001 book: a tube-fed .22 lever gun with a 1/4-cock hammer safety. Henry says the rifle does not need to come apart to be cleaned, and the routine below is the one it prints. The receiver cover comes off only in the deep branch.

steps.title: Hammer to the Safety position, inner magazine tube withdrawn
steps.action: Set the hammer to the Safety position first, then point the muzzle up or in a safe direction and pull the inner magazine tube right out of the gun. Tip the rifle down and let the cartridges run out into a container. The tube is spring-loaded, so keep a hand on the knob as it comes free rather than letting it snap out.
steps.quote: To unload the magazine the hammer should be resting in the Safety position. With the rifle pointing upward or in a safe direction, completely withdraw the inner magazine tube from the gun. Tip the rifle downward, allowing the cartridges to slide out into a suitable container.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO UNLOAD THE MAGAZINE AND CHAMBER OF YOUR HENRY LEVER ACTION RIFLE, p.9

steps.title: Lever cycled repeatedly, chamber looked at
steps.action: Work the lever several times, not once. Emptying the magazine tube does nothing about a round already in the chamber, and a tube gun can still have a cartridge sitting on the carrier. Then put your eye on the chamber — the ejection port is on the side, so roll the rifle until you can see the chamber mouth is bare metal.
steps.caution: Do not dry fire it to prove it is empty.
steps.quote: Cycle the action multiple times to be positive that no live rounds remain in the rifle. Visually inspect the chamber to ensure the rifle is unloaded.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO UNLOAD THE MAGAZINE AND CHAMBER OF YOUR HENRY LEVER ACTION RIFLE, p.10

steps.title: Hammer down, muzzle safe, ammunition out of the room
steps.action: Open the action and confirm the rifle is empty before any solvent comes out, and keep the muzzle pointed somewhere safe the whole time you are working. Henry also wants the ammunition away from where you are cleaning — a loose .22 round on a cluttered bench is the one that finds its way back into the tube.
steps.quote: OPEN THE ACTION AND MAKE CERTAIN YOUR FIREARM IS COMPLETELY UNLOADED. KEEP THE MUZZLE POINTED IN A SAFE DIRECTION.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — CLEANING SAFETY PRECAUTIONS, p.11
steps.warn: KEEP ALL AMMUNITION AWAY FROM THE CLEANING AREA.

steps.title: Rimfire: do not dry fire it
steps.action: Resist the habit of dropping the hammer on an empty chamber. On a rimfire the firing pin strikes the chamber mouth rather than a case rim, and Henry warns that doing it repeatedly peens that edge — the symptom is cartridges that suddenly become stiff to chamber and stiff to extract, and by then the damage is done.
steps.quote: It is suggested that you do NOT dry fire this rifle. Repeated dry firing of a rimfire can eventually peen the edge of the chamber, making it difficult to load and extract cartridges.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO LOAD YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.9

steps.title: Lever cycled forward to open the action, bore and chamber inspected
steps.action: Swing the lever forward to hold the action open — that is as far as this rifle needs to come apart for a normal clean. Look into the chamber and down the bore and note what is actually there: brass, copper and powder fouling all leave different marks. A film of powder residue in a .22 is normal and is not a fault.
steps.aside: A normal amount of powder residue can be expected and is not serious.
steps.quote: For cleaning, we suggest that you first open the action by cycling the lever forward. Inspect the chamber and bore for brass, copper and powder fouling.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO CLEAN YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.12

steps.title: Bore cleaned breech to muzzle, the way the bullet went
steps.action: Pull the patch through from the breech end toward the muzzle, following the bullet. Henry is explicit about the direction and about why: going the other way rakes the fouling out of the barrel and deposits it in the chamber and the action, which is how a clean bore turns into a gritty lever. A pull-through cord suits this rifle because the action opens at the side rather than the rear.
steps.prose: To properly clean from breech to muzzle, use a pull-though cleaning kit, such as those available on www.henrypride.com.
steps.quote: WHENEVER POSSIBLE, CLEAN THE BORE IN THE DIRECTION OF BULLET TRAVEL.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO CLEAN YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.12
steps.warn: Improperly cleaning from muzzle to breech will cause this powder residue to be carried from the bore into the chamber and action, causing fouling of intricate parts and warranting more thorough cleaning by a qualified gunsmith.

steps.title: Fresh patch every pass, brush never reversed in the bore
steps.action: Use a clean face of patch on each trip down the barrel — a patch that has already collected grit just puts it back. If you use a brush, drive it all the way through and off the end before pulling it back; reversing a brush inside the bore folds the bristles over and ruins it, and Henry's comparison is bending a wire back and forth until it snaps.
steps.aside: NEVER RUN A BRUSH IN THE BARREL FIRST.
steps.quote: NOTE: USE A CLEAN PATCH EACH TIME YOU GO DOWN THE BARREL. NEVER GO BACK AND FORTH REVERSING THE BRUSH.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO CLEAN YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.12

steps.title: Solvent measured in drops, not poured
steps.action: Wet the patch and no more than the patch — a few drops is the whole allowance. Excess solvent runs down into the trigger mechanism and leaves it gummy, and excess oil drains back into the wood at the wrist and rots the stock from the inside. On a lever gun both paths are downhill from the breech, so over-wetting always ends up somewhere you did not intend.
steps.caution: If you use too much, the solvent or oil will drip down into the trigger mechanism; this will cause a gummy trigger.
steps.quote: USE ONLY A FEW DROPS OF SOLVENT/LUBRICANT OIL. Use only the amount of solvent that the patch will absorb.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO CLEAN YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.12

steps.title: Bolt wiped and lightly oiled
steps.action: With the action held open, wipe the bolt face and body down with a solvent-damp patch or rag until the carbon ring around the firing-pin hole is gone, then put the lightest film of oil on it. Light is the operative word — a wet bolt in a .22 collects unburnt powder and turns into a grinding paste.
steps.quote: Wipe the bolt clean of any debris with solvent and a patch or small rag. Lightly oil bolt.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO CLEAN YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.12

steps.title: Every exposed metal surface left under a film of oil
steps.action: Finish by wiping a thin film of oil over all the exposed steel — barrel, receiver, lever, magazine tubes. Henry's line is that rust is neglect, not bad luck. If the rifle has been out in damp weather, wipe the bore and the outside dry first and then re-oil, because oil spread over trapped moisture seals the water in rather than keeping it out.
steps.quote: Remember - Rust is neglect. Make sure all exposed metal surfaces are coated with a film of oil.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO CLEAN YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.12

steps.title: Field strip complete
steps.action: That is the whole routine Henry publishes for the H001, and the book is blunt that the rifle does not have to come apart to stay clean. If you want inside the receiver, the Deep Clean branch follows Henry's own receiver-cover procedure — buttstock first, then the cover. Anything past that Henry sends to a gunsmith.
steps.quote: IMPORTANT - PLEASE NOTE THAT IT IS NOT NECESSARY TO TAKE YOUR HENRY LEVER ACTION APART TO KEEP IT CLEAN.
steps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO CLEAN YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.11

deepSteps.title: Receiver cover tang screw out, buttstock off first
deepSteps.action: Henry's order is not optional: the tang screw that runs down through the top of the grip comes out and the buttstock comes off BEFORE anything else. That screw passes through the rear of the receiver cover, so the cover cannot lift while the stock is still bolted to it. Support the stock as the screw clears — it is only held by that one fastener.
deepSteps.caution: Henry identifies this fastener as part #50 and part #55 in its own parts list.
deepSteps.quote: SHOULD YOU WISH TO TAKE IT APART, UNSCREW THE RECEIVER COVER TANG SCREW
deepSteps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO CLEAN YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.11

deepSteps.title: Four receiver cover screws out, cover lifted off
deepSteps.action: With the stock away, take out the four screws holding the receiver cover and lift the cover clear. The internals are underneath and are not captive — lift the cover straight up rather than sliding it, and do it over a tray, because this is the point at which a small part can leave the rifle without you noticing.
deepSteps.quote: THEN UNSCREW THE FOUR RECEIVER COVER SCREWS (PART #42) AND LIFT OFF THE RECEIVER COVER WHICH WILL EXPOSE THE INTERNAL PARTS.
deepSteps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO CLEAN YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.12

deepSteps.title: Exposed internals wiped, nothing further dismantled
deepSteps.action: Clean what the open receiver gives you access to and stop there. Wipe the fouling out of the receiver walls and off the parts you can reach, then re-oil lightly. Henry draws the line at this point explicitly — the fitted inner mechanism is not an owner-level assembly, and taking it further is how a smooth Henry action stops being smooth.
deepSteps.prose: If further disassembly for service or cleaning is required, take your firearm to a qualified gunsmith.
deepSteps.quote: NOTICE! DO NOT ATTEMPT TO TAKE YOUR FIREARM APART FURTHER THAN EXPLAINED IN THIS MANUAL.
deepSteps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — HOW TO CLEAN YOUR HENRY RIFLE, p.11

deepSteps.title: Long storage: bore, chamber and internals oiled, nothing airtight
deepSteps.action: If the rifle is going away for a season, oil the bore, chamber and internal surfaces with a proper firearm preservative and put anti-rust oil on the outside. Do not seal it in anything airtight and do not plug the barrel — both trap moisture against the steel instead of keeping it away. Clean it again before the first shot next season.
deepSteps.quote: If your firearm is to be stored for an extended period, the bore, chamber and internal surfaces should be oiled with a high-quality lubricating oil or preservative intended for firearms.
deepSteps.cite: Henry H001 Series User Manual — undated — no edition, revision or form code is printed in the book — MAINTENANCE BEFORE STORAGE, p.13

cleaning.name: BORE & CHAMBER
tasks: Pull a solvent-damp patch from the breech toward the muzzle, following bullet travel
Repeat with a fresh patch face each pass until the patch comes out clean
Dry the bore, then leave the lightest film of oil in it

cleaning.name: BOLT & ACTION
tasks: Wipe the bolt face and body clean of carbon, then oil lightly
Wipe the carrier and the inside of the receiver window you can reach with the lever open
Keep solvent off the trigger mechanism — it drains downhill and leaves the trigger gummy

cleaning.name: MAGAZINE TUBES & EXTERIOR
tasks: Wipe the inner magazine tube and its follower dry — no heavy oil where cartridges ride
Wipe out the loading port in the outer tube
Leave a film of oil on all exposed steel; wipe the wood with a dry cloth only

reassembly: Set the receiver cover back on and start all four cover screws before tightening any of them.
Refit the buttstock and draw the tang screw down last, so the cover pulls into alignment as it seats.
Reinstall the inner magazine tube until it is fully seated and twist to lock, taking care as it is under spring tension.
Cycle the lever several times by hand and confirm the action runs smoothly through its full travel.
fncheck: With the rifle confirmed empty, cycle the lever fully open and closed several times and confirm the action runs without binding, check the inner magazine tube is fully seated and locked, and confirm the hammer will set into the Safety position and does not fall when the trigger is pulled from it.
